topics.topic: Meaning of “host” and evidence that the actual execution host is Linux
questions: What must the release-process test show to establish that the release runs on Linux and on no other host, rather than merely that its base image is labelled Linux? A21 says test 5 shows the host, but this item checks only the base image and Python.

What does “host” mean for the required refusal: the physical home-server OS, the VM Platform guest/kernel that executes Registry, or merely the operating-system identity of the base image; and what must test 5 show about that host rather than only about the base image?

Does “host” mean the Registry guest or container environment fixed by the base image, the VM Platform guest operating system, or the physical or hypervisor host; and which of those must be Linux for the release to be allowed?
How must required test 5 show that the actual host on which the release runs is Linux, when the test as written checks only that the base image is a Linux one?

   libraries and the store's engine.

consequences: The same Linux image running in a Linux guest on a non-Linux physical host is admitted or refused depending on the unresolved meaning of host.

topics.topic: Authoritative Linux and file-system semantics defining the supported-host boundary
questions: Which exact documented semantics must a Linux host and its file system provide for the deployment to be supported, and which document or conformance profile decides this when Linux, a file-system manual and a storage layer give different or qualified guarantees?

Which Linux documentation and semantics determine whether a kernel, file system, mount configuration, or call result is supported, especially where durability and atomicity guarantees vary by file system, mount options, kernel version, or whether a containing directory is flushed?

quotes:
Another system, or a Linux or
   file system on which a call Registry's rules rely on — opening a file
   without following a link, binding a listening socket, renaming, flushing
   — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: Registry neither
   tests for it nor defines what it does there.

Under
 files_artifacts (A16, A18), opening without following a link is Linux's.
 Under concurrency (A17, A18), binding each listener exclusively and
 renaming and flushing a backup are Linux's.

Second, it
   writes the backup under a temporary name and checks it: it decrypts it
   into a second temporary file, opens that for reading only, checks that it
   is the store version of its release, that the full integrity check (A17
   rule 5)
   passes and that the last sequence number it keeps (A15) equals the
   recorded one, and
   removes it; a backup that passes is renamed to its kept name, one that
   fails is deleted.

every backup, when it becomes kept, is encrypted, consistent, checked, and
records (instant, release, last sequence); no backup holds an agent
session   -- A18-2
judgement.divergence: One interpretation classifies the mounted file system as supported because its calls satisfy a generic Linux description, while another classifies it as unsupported because its documented file-system or mount semantics do not supply the relied-on rename or flush guarantee; the owner observes whether A18-2 is promised for the resulting backup, and claiming support where the authoritative semantics are not met violates the stated support boundary.
judgement.why: State 2 makes its file, listener and backup guarantees depend on Linux-documented behavior but does not identify the authoritative documentation or required semantics that separate supported from unsupported environments.
options: Enumerate the relied-on semantics and every precondition for no-follow opening, exclusive binding, atomic rename and durable flushing.
Name a fixed Linux documentation set or conformance profile as authoritative.
Use the documentation of the selected kernel, file system and mount configuration.
Treat every environment identifying itself as Linux as supported regardless of operation-specific qualifications.
consequences: Different release operators can classify the same kernel, file system and mount configuration differently.
A deployment may be promised backup, file-safety and exclusive-binding guarantees under one interpretation but be outside all Registry guarantees under another.

author_guidance: Before editing, identify the decision's owning state from the phase purpose, question_scope and layer obligations, then choose a disposition for each topic that awaits one.
fixed: repair a decision the owning state must make; do not add later-layer implementation choices merely to close a topic. Record the fix commit and review the changed text once.

carried: name the receiving layer and use --what to preserve the choice, its options and consequences, and the required guarantee every option must keep. Decide any guarantee owned here before carrying its execution onward.
accepted: explain why the remaining choice is permitted. Bring an unresolved product choice to the owner with its options and consequences; absence of a quoted requirement does not decide it.
contradiction and standard_violation take no disposition: repair the offending text in its owning state and review the change. Deterministic transition findings must also close through their checks.
State 2: decide required results and constraints, including necessary refusal precedence; carry test mechanisms, exact contracts and deployment procedures to their owners.
